subsystems.name: Starlight-suppression optics
subsystems.role: hides the host star so a planet's faint light can be separated from it.

subsystems.name: Large-aperture telescope
subsystems.role: collects enough photons: a city-lights signal is extraordinarily faint.

subsystems.name: Photometer and detectors
subsystems.role: counts photons precisely enough to see a nightside excess.

subsystems.name: Phase-curve observation mode
subsystems.role: watches a planet through its whole orbit to separate dayside from nightside.

subsystems.name: Spectral comparison library
subsystems.role: tests whether a residual spectrum looks artificial rather than natural.
parts: model spectra of city lighting (e.g. sodium and LED-like bands)
natural-source spectra: volcanism, lightning, aurorae, airglow

subsystems.name: Analysis pipeline
subsystems.role: subtracts star, thermal emission and reflected light to leave a residual.

buildSteps.title: Pick targets where the test is cleanest
buildSteps.detail: Favour nearby, temperate planets — especially tidally locked ones, whose permanent night hemisphere has no reflected starlight at all, so any visible flux must be thermal or artificial.

buildSteps.title: Predict the signal
buildSteps.detail: Model how bright a city-covered hemisphere would be at 0.4–1.0 µm, and compare that with the planet's own thermal emission at the same wavelengths, which for a temperate planet is very small.

buildSteps.title: Suppress the star
buildSteps.detail: Two routes: for transiting planets, use eclipse and phase-curve photometry so the star's light is subtracted rather than blocked optically; for direct imaging, use a coronagraph or a starshade to reach contrasts of roughly one part in ten billion.

buildSteps.title: Observe a full orbit
buildSteps.detail: Stare continuously through the orbit so the changing fraction of lit hemisphere can be fitted, with the nightside measured just before and after transit.

buildSteps.title: Extract the nightside residual
buildSteps.detail: Remove stellar flux, reflected light, thermal emission and known instrument drifts, leaving a small excess or upper limit.

buildSteps.title: Compare spectra, not just brightness
buildSteps.detail: Artificial lighting has a distinctive spectral shape with sharp features; a smooth thermal continuum points to a hot planet or volcano instead.

buildSteps.title: Rule out natural sources
buildSteps.detail: Check for variability, polarisation and correlation with known geology that would indicate aurorae, lightning, volcanic lava or atmospheric airglow.

buildSteps.title: Confirm with repeats
buildSteps.detail: Repeat observations over multiple orbits and, later, use a larger telescope for spectroscopy to see whether the spectral features persist.

prerequisites.why: existing coronagraphs reach about 1e-6 to 1e-7 on bright stars; a terrestrial planet needs several orders of magnitude more.
space telescopes now measure exoplanet phase curves precisely, but detecting a nightside excess is far harder.
a dedicated 6–8 m-class space observatory with coronagraphy has been studied but not built.
models of what a city-lit or volcanically lit hemisphere looks like are still approximate.
the temperature map of a planet must be known well enough to subtract its own glow.

pathway.milestone: theoretical detectability studies and, for hot planets, precise phase-curve spectroscopy
pathway.unlocks: proof that nightside fluxes can be measured at all, though not yet at city-light sensitivity.

pathway.milestone: extremely large ground telescopes with extreme adaptive optics and coronagraphs
pathway.unlocks: direct imaging of nearby gas giants and the brightest rocky planets.

pathway.milestone: a space telescope with a coronagraph or starshade reaching 1e-10 contrast
pathway.unlocks: reflected-light spectra of temperate terrestrial planets, and with them a real nightside test.

pathway.milestone: a survey of the nearest terrestrial planets for nightside illumination excesses
pathway.unlocks: either a candidate technosignature or a strong upper limit on city-scale lighting nearby.
